newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Copper at one year high, coffee wilts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Copper at one year high, coffee wilts.

text.p: Investors in commodity markets were warmed by a sharp rise in copper prices on Wednesday but rising temperatures in Brazil sent coffee prices in the opposite direction.
London Metal Exchange (LME) copper three months delivery futures rose $35 a tonne in early trade to stand at $2,550, the highest level seen for a year.
Brokers GNI in a daily market report cited positive charts and falling stocks of the metal as factors behind the market's rise.
Followers of charts reckoned that the point reached at Tuesday's close signalled a sure bet for higher prices at Wednesday's opening.
"Copper has closed positively on the highs....the next level of resistance is between $2,440/$2,450," brokers Rudolf Wolff said late Tuesday.
Some watchers of the market's fundamentals are worried that falling stocks could prove a problem to the industry during the summer, particularly if China needs to import.
Total stocks in LME warehouses are 127,525 tonnes and less than half of these are housed in facilities in the important European market, where there is a shortage of good quality metal, traders said.
Just under 20,000 tonnes are in the Singapore warehouse, the nearest LME facility to China.
North American stocks could come under pressure if a strike at Canadian producer Inco Ltd's Sudbury, Ontario, facilities which produce 90,000 tonnes of copper, becomes a lengthy affair.

Equity traders were also getting excited about copper and piled into shares of Rio Tinto Plc after a month-old report from Bankers Trust forecasting copper reaching $3,000 a tonne by the year end was regurgitated in the British press.
London robust coffee futures prices fell around $150 a tonne on Wednesday morning with the July futures position touching $1,675 which represented a 37 percent drop from the late May peak of $2,670.

Fears of already extreme supply tightness, due to producer restricting exports, possibly being exacerbated by frost hitting the coffee growing areas or world number one producer Brazil appeared to have dissipated for the time being.

"I think it's lacking buyers," said Steve Platt an analyst at brokers Dean Whitter in the U.S. "There has been a loosening of supply availability as Brazil's harvest proceeds and some....comes out of Colombia."
In addition independent U.S. weather forecaster said that no dmaging cold is expected through early next week in Brazil's coffee regions.
Conditions are generally favourable, with rains last week boosting soil moisture ahead of the winter dry season, WSC said.
In 1994 frost followed by drought during the Brazilian winter seriously hit coffee production.
Among other commodities, the rest of the industrial metals complex was being underpinned by copper's impressive performance while in the precious metals, platinum and palladium were more stable.

They had recently moved to highest levels seen for many years on extreme supply tightness caused by a lack of Russian exports in 1997 due to bureaucratic delays, which at one stage raised fears of possible defaults in the market.
"The panic is dying down and dealers are trying to be responsible and keep the market trading," a broker said.
